name: Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation
title: Historical Role Play, Labeled as Simulation
answer: Historical role play with AI lets students interview or debate simulated historical figures, but only when every simulation is clearly labeled as a simulation and every quote or claim is checked against a real source. It matters because the same activity that builds curiosity about the past can spread invented quotes and false history if it is used carelessly. The teacher decides whether a simulation is appropriate at all, and some figures and events are best left to real testimony.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: This idea uses AI to let students talk with a simulated historical figure, debate a simulated delegate at a constitutional convention, or question a simulated witness to an event. The purpose is to make the past feel lived by real people and to build student curiosity. The problem it solves is that history can seem distant and abstract, and role play closes that distance. The risk it creates is that a program imagining a person can produce invented quotes and false history that students then treat as real. The rules of labeling and source checking exist to keep the benefit and remove the danger.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, the teacher sets up the simulation and tests it before class, looking for obvious errors. During the activity, every simulation is labeled clearly as a simulation so students understand they are talking to a program imagining a person, not the person. Any quote or claim a student wants to use must then be checked against a real source. The text does not give separate grade band versions, so the same routine applies wherever role play is used. The teacher also decides in advance which figures and events are suitable for simulation and which are not.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, and the guidance comes from the stated risks of role play and the rules the book sets out for using it. The book's own claim is practical: used carefully, these activities build curiosity and help students see the past as lived by real people, and used carelessly, they spread invented quotes and false history.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are strict. Every simulation must be labeled as a simulation, and no quote or claim can be used until it is checked against a real source. The teacher sets up and tests the simulation before class and looks for obvious errors. Some figures and events need extra caution, because simulating people who suffered great injustice, such as enslaved people or victims of genocide, risks trivializing their experience or putting words in their mouths. Many teachers avoid these simulations entirely and use real testimony instead, and the decision about whether a simulation respects the people it represents stays with the teacher.
